281.title: The battle inside
281.hook: the fiercest fight in the Granth is with the five thieves in your own mind
281.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of the five thieves (kaam, krodh, lobh, moh, ahankar) as the real enemies, and fight them through naam simran, the sangat, the Guru's word, honest work and humility.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nihangs, keeping the old ways alive. A week of swords, flags and horsemen. Today, the last day of sword and saint, and the fight the Guru Granth Sahib keeps coming back to.

No army, no siege, no broken oath. Just an ordinary day that went wrong from the inside: a snapped word at someone loved, an hour scrolled away that wasn't there to spare, a grab for the bigger slice, the last word, the credit. For a week this path has talked about swords. Open the Guru Granth Sahib looking for battles, though, and the ones it keeps returning to have no armies in them. Its fiercest fight happens somewhere else. Today: the battle inside.
screen: `NO ARMY, NO SIEGE.` → `A DAY LOST FROM THE INSIDE.` → `THE FIERCEST FIGHT IS ELSEWHERE.`

segments.voice: The Granth names the enemy many times, and it has five faces: kaam, desire that grabs; krodh, anger; lobh, greed; moh, clinging to what we can't keep; and ahankar, pride. These are the five thieves you met weeks ago. Today, the line that turns them into a battle. It's in Guru Nanak's Japji, the morning prayer, in the twenty-eighth verse. That verse speaks to the yogis of Guru Nanak's day and turns their outward gear inward: make contentment your earrings, meditation the ash on your body, faith your staff. Then it closes on a short line: man jeetai jag jeet. Conquer your own mind, and you've conquered the world. Hold that up against this whole week. The saint-soldier's courage. The kirpan, mercy first. Every other means first. Fair, even in conflict. The calm face in gatka. Each one depends on winning an inner fight first: against anger that wants to strike, pride that wants to win, fear that wants to run. A soldier who hasn't fought the five thieves isn't a saint-soldier, just a soldier. The Granth's weapons for this fight aren't steel. The Name, remembered. The sangat, the company of good people. The Guru's word. Honest work and sharing. And humility, the opposite of ahankar. Sikhs don't speak of winning it once and for all. It's a daily fight, and the wins are often small: one sharp word not said, one craving let pass. That's the battle the whole week pointed to.
screen: `THE FIVE THIEVES, MET AGAIN.` · `JAPJI 28: THE YOGI'S GEAR TURNED INWARD.` · `CONQUER THE MIND, CONQUER THE WORLD.` · `THE WEAPONS: NAME, SANGAT, HUMILITY.` · then, large: `THE REAL BATTLE.`

segments.voice: Take an honest look inward: which of the five is loudest in you today, anger, greed, desire, clinging or pride? Don't fight it yet; just name it quietly, the way you'd name a visitor. Then choose one small win against it: one word you won't say, or one thing you'll let go of.
Ahankar. Pride, one of the five thieves that wage the battle inside; conquer your own mind, and you've conquered the world.
Your line: the real battle. Its weapons aren't steel. That closes sword and saint, on day two hundred eighty-one.

282.title: Banda Singh Bahadur
282.hook: an ascetic from the south meets Guru Gobind Singh at Nanded and becomes the Khalsa's commander
282.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Banda Singh Bahadur as the commander Guru Gobind Singh sent to lead the Khalsa in Punjab; the gurdwara at Nanded, Hazur Sahib, is one of the five takhts, marking where Guru Gobind Singh spent his last days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ahankar, and the real battle with the five thieves inside. That closed sword and saint. Today a long new stretch begins: Sikh history after the Gurus.

Nanded, on the banks of the Godavari river, deep in the south of India, 1708. A holy man lives in a hermitage there. He has left the world behind: no family, no possessions, many followers, and a reputation for strange powers. People say visitors who sit on his special seat get tipped off it. One day he comes home and finds a stranger sitting on that seat, completely at ease. The stranger is Guru Gobind Singh.
screen: `NANDED, ON THE GODAVARI, 1708.` → `A HERMIT WITH A SPECIAL SEAT.` → `A STRANGER SITTING ON IT.`

segments.voice: The hermit's story, as tradition tells it, started far from Nanded. He was born in 1670 in the hills near Kashmir and named Lachhman Dev. As a young man, the story goes, he went hunting and killed a doe, and watched her unborn young die with her. It shook him so badly that he gave up the world and became a wandering ascetic, Madho Das, and ended up in the south, at Nanded. Guru Gobind Singh had come south too, after losing his sons and his city. Tradition says Madho Das tried his powers on the Guru, and they did nothing. Shaken, he asked who this was. Then he said, in effect: I am your banda. Banda means servant, one bound to another. He took amrit, and the name that stuck was Banda Singh. Later people added Bahadur, the brave. Here's the turn. The Guru didn't ask Banda to go deeper into his hermitage. He sent him out: to Punjab, where the Sikhs were being crushed and the killers of the Guru's young sons still held power. Tradition says the Guru gave him five arrows from his own quiver, a flag, a drum, and a small band of Sikhs, with letters asking the Khalsa to rally behind him. The Guru himself died at Nanded later that year. So the man who'd walked away from the world was sent straight back into it. For Sikhs, Banda's story is a picture of what a call can do. Sometimes the service asked of you is the thing you'd left behind.

segments.voice: Think of a direction you've been walking in for a while, a habit, a job, a way of spending evenings or of treating someone, and ask it honestly: is this where I'm needed? Banda. A servant, one bound to another — the name the hermit Madho Das took when he pledged himself to Guru Gobind Singh and was sent to lead the Khalsa.
Your line: called to serve. From hermit to servant, then sent out to lead. See you in Punjab tomorrow.

283.title: Sirhind, 1710
283.hook: Banda's forces take Sirhind, and land is given to those who till it
283.howItsDone: Each December, Sikhs gather in large numbers at Gurdwara Fatehgarh Sahib near Sirhind for the Shaheedi Jor Mela, remembering the martyrdom of Guru Gobind Singh's youngest sons; Banda's victory of 1710 is remembered alongside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Banda, the hermit sent back into the world to serve. Today, Banda reaches Punjab, and the city everyone was watching.

A farmer plows land his family has worked for generations. He plants it, brings in the harvest, then watches a large share go to a landlord who has never touched the soil, and another share go in taxes. What's left barely feeds his children. Then a rider comes to the village with news: the land now belongs to the people who work it. For many Punjabi farmers in 1710, something like that happened. It began at a city with a painful name in Sikh memory. Today: Sirhind.
screen: `LAND A FAMILY HAS WORKED FOR GENERATIONS.` → `A LANDLORD WHO NEVER TOUCHED IT.` → `THE LAND BELONGS TO THOSE WHO WORK IT.`

segments.voice: Sirhind was a rich Mughal city on the road between Delhi and Lahore, governed by Wazir Khan. A few years earlier, it was in Sirhind, under his authority, that Guru Gobind Singh's two youngest sons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, were executed. They were small boys. Sikhs everywhere knew that name. When Banda Singh Bahadur arrived in Punjab with the Guru's arrows and letters, thousands joined him, many of them poor farmers. In May 1710, at a place called Chappar Chiri, his forces met Wazir Khan's army. Wazir Khan was killed, and the Sikhs took Sirhind. Historians record that the city was sacked, and that many of its people suffered. That's part of the honest story too. Then Banda did something that made him remembered far beyond the battlefield. He set up his own rule, with a fort called Lohgarh, and struck coins in the names of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh, not his own. And in the lands he held, he broke the power of the big landlords, the zamindars, and let the land go to those who actually tilled it. How complete that change was, and how long it lasted, historians still debate. But for farmers in Banda's lands, for a time, the soil under their feet was their own. Today a great gurdwara, Fatehgarh Sahib, stands at Sirhind where the young sons died. Every December, Sikhs go there in their thousands to remember them. Victory at Sirhind is remembered with that grief, not instead of it.

Your line: land to the tillers. A victory, remembered with grief. That's two hundred eighty-three days.

284.title: Banda's end, 1716
284.hook: captured with hundreds of Sikhs, Banda is executed in Delhi without renouncing his faith
284.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Banda Singh Bahadur and the Sikhs executed with him in Delhi in 1716 as shaheeds, martyrs; Ardas, said daily, honors those who gave their lives rather than give up their faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sirhind, and land to the tillers: Banda's rise. Today is harder: how it ended. It's told carefully, and you can take it slowly.

Just say you didn't mean it. Just sign here. Just go along, and this all goes away. An easy way out usually comes with small stakes: a grade, a job, a friendship. Now raise the stakes. The easy way out is your life, and all it costs is saying you no longer believe what you believe. In the spring of 1716, in Delhi, hundreds of Sikhs were offered exactly that.
screen: `JUST SAY YOU DIDN'T MEAN IT.` → `THE EASY WAY OUT.` → `DELHI, 1716.`

segments.voice: After Sirhind, the Mughal empire turned its full weight on Banda. For five years he fought and retreated through the hills and plains of Punjab. In 1715 his forces were surrounded at a walled compound near the village of Gurdas Nangal. The siege lasted about eight months. Food ran out; people ate leaves and bark. In December, starving, they were captured. Banda and hundreds of Sikhs were marched to Delhi in chains and paraded through the streets. Then, for about a week, a group was executed each day. Each was offered life if they gave up their faith. Accounts, including a letter written at the time by two English envoys in Delhi, say not one of them accepted. Sikhs tell a story from those days. A mother pleaded for her young son, saying he wasn't really a Sikh, and won a pardon. The boy refused it. His mother was mistaken, he said; he was a Sikh, and he would stand with the others. In June 1716, Banda himself was executed, after being forced to watch his small son killed before him. He did not renounce his faith. It's a terrible story, and Sikhs don't tell it for thrills. They tell it the way a family remembers its hardest year. It's part of why Ardas, the daily Sikh prayer, remembers those who gave their lives rather than give up their faith. The question it leaves isn't, could I survive that? Almost none of us will face it. It's a smaller one. When the easy way out is offered, what am I true to?
screen: `GURDAS NANGAL — EIGHT MONTHS' SIEGE.` · `DELHI — LIFE OFFERED FOR THE FAITH.` · `NOT ONE ACCEPTED.` · `REMEMBERED IN ARDAS.` · then, large: `TRUE TO THE END.`

Banda's end. Captured after a long siege, Banda and hundreds of Sikhs were executed in Delhi in 1716, and none gave up their faith to live.
Your line: true to the end. Not one of them accepted. Day two hundred eighty-four.

285.title: The years in the forests
285.hook: a price is set on Sikh heads and the Khalsa survives in jungles and deserts
285.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the eighteenth-century years of persecution in Ardas and in stories told at gurdwaras; the Khalsa's playful coded speech from that time, sometimes called Khalsa bole, is still used by Nihangs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Banda's end in Delhi: true to the end. With their leader gone, how did the Sikhs go on?

The thick scrub forest of central Punjab, after dark. No roads, no lamps. A few riders move through it quietly, horses tied in the undergrowth, supper cooking on a low fire that won't be seen from the plain. Back in the towns, a notice has gone up: a reward for every Sikh brought in, alive or dead. These riders have left everything. And around the fire, surprisingly, somebody is laughing.
screen: `SCRUB FOREST, AFTER DARK.` → `A REWARD FOR EVERY SIKH.` → `AROUND THE FIRE, LAUGHTER.`

segments.voice: After 1716, the Mughal governors of Punjab set out to finish the Khalsa. For long stretches over the next decades, a price was put on Sikh heads, and people were rewarded for turning them in. Being recognized as a Sikh, with uncut hair and a turban, could cost you your life. Some Sikhs cut their hair and stayed in the villages. Many of the Khalsa went where soldiers couldn't easily follow: the scrub jungles of Punjab, the foothills of the Himalaya, the edges of the Rajasthan desert. They moved in small bands, lived on what they could find or what villagers quietly gave them, and struck back when they could. And they kept coming home in secret. Tradition says riders would slip into Amritsar by night to bathe in the pool at the Harmandir, and be gone before morning. What kept them going? Faith, first: daily prayers said in the open air, the Guru Granth Sahib honored even in a camp. And a fierce, stubborn humor. The Khalsa built up its own playful way of talking. One rider on his own might call himself an army. Plain rough food got grand names. Tradition credits Guru Gobind Singh with the saying that one Sikh would stand against sava lakh, a hundred and twenty-five thousand, and the riders took it at its word, with a grin. In 1733 the government in Lahore, unable to finish them, offered the Khalsa a truce, land and the title of Nawab. The Khalsa gave the title to Kapur Singh, who was fanning the sangat when the offer came. The truce didn't last, and harder years were coming. But a small, hunted people, living under the stars for decades, wasn't crushed. They survived.
screen: `A PRICE ON SIKH HEADS.` · `JUNGLES, HILLS AND DESERTS.` · `SECRET NIGHTS AT THE POOL.` · `ONE RIDER IS SAVA LAKH.` · then, large: `THEY SURVIVED.`

segments.voice: Look around the room you're in, the walls, the roof, the door you can lock, and notice one thing that keeps you safe and warm. Then think of the riders in the scrub, and of anyone tonight with no safe place to sleep, and let gratitude for your shelter rise, without guilt. If you pray, you can hold them in it.
Sava lakh. One and a quarter lakh, 125,000, the number one Sikh is said to stand against; the hunted Khalsa took it at its word, with a grin, and survived.
Your line: they survived. Hunted for decades, and still laughing around the fire. Until tomorrow, then.

286.title: Bhai Mani Singh, 1734
286.hook: the scribe and granthi of the Harmandir is executed for his faith
286.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Mani Singh in Ardas among those cut joint by joint for their faith; a gurdwara in Lahore marks the place of his execution, and Damdama Sahib, where tradition says he wrote out the Granth, is one of the five takhts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sava lakh, the years in the forests: they survived. While riders hid in the scrub, one old man stayed in plain sight, at the Harmandir.

A pen moves across a page, slowly, while a voice recites hymns aloud, line after line. Sikh tradition says this is how the Guru Granth Sahib took its final form: Guru Gobind Singh reciting, and one devoted Sikh writing down every word. The writer was a scholar, not a soldier. Years later he became the keeper of the Harmandir. And the daily Sikh prayer still recalls the way he died. Today: Bhai Mani Singh.
screen: `A PEN, A VOICE, LINE AFTER LINE.` → `A WHOLE HOLY BOOK, BY HAND.` → `A SCHOLAR, NOT A SOLDIER.`

segments.voice: Bhai means brother, the title Sikhs give to someone respected for their devotion. Tradition says Mani Singh grew up alongside Guru Gobind Singh and served him all his life. At Damdama Sahib, in 1706, tradition says the Guru dictated the whole Granth, adding his father Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns, and Bhai Mani Singh wrote it out. That's the form of the scripture Sikhs honor as the Guru today. Years later he was sent to Amritsar as granthi of the Harmandir, the keeper and reader of the Guru Granth Sahib. The Sikhs there had split into two rival camps. Tradition says he settled it without a blow: each side wrote its claim on a slip, the slips went into the sacred pool, and the side whose slip floated would take charge. One floated, the other sank, and the dispute ended. Then came the hard years. In the 1730s he asked the governor in Lahore for permission to hold a great Diwali gathering at Amritsar, and agreed to pay a heavy fee. Word spread that soldiers would attack the gathering, so few Sikhs dared come, and the fee couldn't be paid. He was arrested. Offered his life if he gave up his faith, the old scribe refused. He was executed in Lahore, cut apart joint by joint. Ardas remembers those who were cut joint by joint and did not give up their faith, and Sikhs hear his name in those words. The sources don't agree on the year. The title's 1734 is one date given; other histories say 1737 or 1738. What they agree on is the man.

287.title: Bhai Taru Singh, 1745
287.hook: a young farmer who fed travelers refuses to cut his hair even under torture
287.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Taru Singh in Ardas among those who gave their scalps rather than their kesh; a gurdwara, Shaheed Ganj Bhai Taru Singh, marks the place in Lahore, and his story is often told to children to explain why Sikhs keep their hair.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhai: the scribe stood firm. Today, a farmer, and the end of a hard week of history, with a look back at it.

A knock at the door, late at night. On the step, two strangers, thin, dusty, clearly on the run. Everyone in the village knows feeding people like this is dangerous. Somebody might be watching. Somebody might talk. You could say you have nothing and close the door, and nobody would ever blame you. In a small village near Lahore in the 1740s, a young farmer heard knocks like that again and again. He never closed the door. Today: Bhai Taru Singh.
screen: `A KNOCK AT THE DOOR, LATE.` → `STRANGERS ON THE RUN.` → `HE NEVER CLOSED THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Taru Singh was a young farmer who lived with his mother and sister in Poohla, a village not far from Lahore. These were the years of the price on Sikh heads. The Khalsa bands hid in the jungles, and they needed food. Taru Singh grew grain and shared it. Travelers, hunted Sikhs, anyone hungry at the door: tradition says his household fed them all, from the little they had. Someone informed on him. In 1745 he was arrested and brought before the governor in Lahore, charged with feeding the rebels. He was offered his life if he gave up his faith and cut his hair. He said his kesh, his uncut hair, was part of his faith, and he would keep it along with his life's breath. The governor's men removed his scalp. Tradition says he bore it with his lips moving in prayer, and died soon after. Sikhs remember him in Ardas among those who were scalped rather than give up their kesh. You'll remember kesh from the five Ks: hair kept as it was given. For Taru Singh it wasn't a rule. It was himself. Now, the week. The battle inside: the real battle. Banda Singh Bahadur: called to serve. Sirhind: land to the tillers. Banda's end: true to the end. The years in the forests: they survived. Bhai Mani Singh: the scribe stood firm. And Bhai Taru Singh, the farmer who kept feeding strangers, and kept his kesh.
screen: `A FARMER WHO FED THE HUNTED.` · `ARRESTED FOR FEEDING THE REBELS.` · `CUT YOUR HAIR, OR DIE.` · `REMEMBERED IN ARDAS.` · then, large: `HE KEPT HIS KESH.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who could use a meal right now: a friend with a new baby, a coworker on a long shift, a neighbor living alone, someone passing through a hard stretch. Picture them at your door, and what you'd set in front of them, a meal, a snack, a coffee, a place at your table. Stay with that open door for a few quiet breaths.
Kesh. Uncut hair, part of the faith of Bhai Taru Singh, the young farmer who fed hunted Sikhs and travelers, and in 1745 refused to cut it to save his life.
Your line: he kept his kesh. And he never closed the door. That's the week, and day two hundred eighty-seven.
